full_title: PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE, VS. RUDY PERALTA Y MABBONAG, CESAR LIBAN Y PERALTA, PHILIP SORIANO Y PASION, ADVIENTO SORIANO Y PASION, ROBERTO SORIANO Y PASION, FERDINAND SORIANO Y PASION ALIAS 'MAR,' AND NAPOLEON LIBAN (AT LARGE), ACCUSED; RUDY PERALTA Y MABBONAG AND CESAR LIBAN Y PERALTA, ACCUSED-APPELLANTS.
subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
syllabus_topic: VII. Criminal Procedure > B. Prosecution of Offenses (Rule 110) > 6. Complaint or Information > d. Amendment and Substitution
topics: Amendment of an information before plea: a matter of right, with no leave and no order of admission needed
Amended information ipso facto supersedes the original
Frustrated murder to murder after the victim's death is a formal amendment (Teehankee, Jr. v. Madayag)
No re-arraignment needed for a formal amendment
Death of an accused pending appeal extinguishes criminal liability and civil liability ex delicto

other_subjects.subject: Criminal Law
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: II. The Revised Penal Code – Book One > D. Extinction of Criminal Liability > 1. Total Extinction > a. Death of Convict

doctrine:
**Before the accused pleads, an information may be amended in form or in substance without leave of court, and the amended information ipso facto supersedes the original. No motion to admit it and no order admitting it are needed** (Rule 110, Section 14, Rules of Court). The exception is an amendment before plea that downgrades the nature of the offense or excludes an accused. That kind of amendment may be made only on the prosecutor's motion, with notice to the offended party and with leave of court. The Court likened the rule to a plaintiff's right to amend a complaint before a responsive pleading is served, where the amended pleading supersedes the original without an order of admission (Rule 10, Section 8). A later court order "admitting" such an amended information is "a superfluity."

**Changing an information from frustrated murder to murder after the victim dies is only a formal amendment.** Frustrated murder is a stage in the execution of murder and is necessarily included in it. The victim's death is a supervening fact that bears only on the penalty, and every defense available under the original information remains available (reiterating *Teehankee, Jr. v. Madayag*). Such an amendment needs no new preliminary investigation and **no re-arraignment**. The purpose of arraignment, to inform the accused of the nature and cause of the accusation, was already served at the first arraignment.

When an accused-appellant dies before final judgment, his criminal liability and his civil liability ex delicto are totally extinguished (Article 89(1), Revised Penal Code; *People v. Bayotas*). Claims for civil liability based on other sources of obligation are not affected.
facts:
On or about June 11, 1994, in Baggao, Cagayan, an armed group that included Rudy Peralta and Cesar Liban went to the house of Virgilio Remigio. They ordered AAA to knock on the door and tell Virgilio that policemen were with her, and one of the group shot Virgilio and his son. An Information dated September 30, 1994 (Criminal Case No. 6621) charged Peralta, Liban and others with frustrated murder. It alleged conspiracy, intent to kill, evident premeditation, treachery and the aggravating circumstance of dwelling. Virgilio died on November 19, 1994. The prosecution then filed an Amended Information dated January 26, 1995 charging the same accused with murder, with the same allegations plus the fact of death.

Peralta's certificate of arraignment shows that he pleaded not guilty on January 30, 1995 to "the crime charged," without naming the crime. Liban, who had been at large, pleaded not guilty to murder on June 24, 1999. At trial, co-accused Lito Acierto was discharged as a state witness and testified to the events of that night.

After the prosecution rested, the defense filed a demurrer to evidence. Among other things, it argued that the RTC never admitted the Amended Information, so the accused could be tried only for frustrated murder. The RTC denied the demurrer on August 30, 2007. In an Order dated September 10, 2007, it then admitted the Amended Information and set a new arraignment. The PAO moved for reconsideration, invoking the right to speedy trial and double jeopardy; the records show no resolution of that motion. At trial, Peralta and Liban each testified that they were at home that night.

In its August 24, 2010 Judgment, the RTC convicted Peralta, Liban and Philip Soriano of murder in Criminal Case No. 6621. It imposed reclusion perpetua and awarded PHP 50,000.00 civil indemnity, PHP 50,000.00 moral damages and PHP 100,000.00 actual damages. On appeal, the accused argued that they had pleaded only to frustrated murder. The CA affirmed on March 19, 2014 (CA-G.R. CR-H.C. No. 04713) and added 6% legal interest. Peralta and Liban appealed to the Supreme Court; Philip did not. Peralta died on October 25, 2023, while the appeal was pending.
issues: Whether Peralta's death pending appeal extinguished his criminal liability and his civil liability ex delicto.
Whether the prosecution proved Liban's guilt for murder beyond reasonable doubt.
Whether Liban could be convicted of murder although the RTC issued an order admitting the Amended Information only in 2007, and the accused claimed they were arraigned only for frustrated murder.
Whether the penalty and damages imposed were correct.
ruling:
**1. Yes.** Peralta died on October 25, 2023, before final judgment. Under Article 89(1) of the Revised Penal Code, his criminal liability is totally extinguished, and the dismissal of Criminal Case No. 6621 as to him follows as a matter of course. His civil liability ex delicto is also extinguished, but claims for civil liability based on other sources of obligation, if any, remain unaffected (*People v. Bayotas*).

**2. Yes.** The Court found no reason to reverse the CA as to Liban. The elements of murder were proved. Only one malefactor shot Virgilio, but conspiracy was proved and may be inferred from the accused's concerted acts, since they arrived at the scene together and fully armed. Their alibi was inherently weak against their positive identification by credible witnesses, and the trial court's findings deserve the highest respect.

**3. Yes, the murder conviction stands, and no order admitting the Amended Information was needed.** Under Rule 110, Section 14, an information may be amended in form or substance without leave of court at any time before the accused pleads. "Without leave of court" means the prosecution need not ask the court's permission to amend before plea, as long as the amendment does not downgrade the offense or exclude an accused. This works like a civil complaint amended as a matter of right (Rule 10, Section 8): **the amended information ipso facto supersedes the original, without a motion to admit it and without further action from the court.** The RTC's 2007 Order admitting the Amended Information was therefore "a superfluity." It did not dismiss the original Information, which the 1995 amendment had already superseded. The accused also never moved to quash the Amended Information, and their own notice of appeal called the case one "for murder."

In any case, the amendment was merely formal. Quoting *Teehankee, Jr. v. Madayag*, the Court explained that frustrated murder is a stage in the execution of murder and is necessarily included in it. The supervening fact of death only helps the court fix the penalty. The prosecution's theory, a felonious act done with intent to kill, stays the same, and any defense under the original information applies equally to the amended one. **Even if the accused had pleaded only to frustrated murder, re-arraignment was unnecessary, because a formal amendment does not require a second arraignment.** The purpose of arraignment was achieved at the first arraignment. The amendment could not have surprised the accused, since it charged no new offense and did not change the prosecution's theory.

**4. The penalty was affirmed, and the damages were modified.** Murder is punished by reclusion perpetua to death. The ordinary aggravating circumstance of dwelling would have warranted death, but Republic Act No. 9346 prohibits the death penalty, so the RTC correctly imposed reclusion perpetua. Under the Court's guidelines on non-eligibility for parole, the Court added the phrase "without eligibility for parole." It raised civil indemnity and moral damages to PHP 100,000.00 each and added PHP 100,000.00 exemplary damages (*People v. Jugueta*). Because no evidence of burial or funeral expenses was presented, it replaced the PHP 100,000.00 actual damages with PHP 50,000.00 temperate damages.
disposition: The appeal was DISMISSED. The CA Decision dated March 19, 2014 in CA-G.R. CR-H.C. No. 04713 was AFFIRMED with MODIFICATION as to Cesar Liban y Peralta. In Criminal Case No. 6621, he was found GUILTY beyond reasonable doubt of murder and sentenced to reclusion perpetua without eligibility for parole. He was ordered to pay the heirs of Virgilio Remigio PHP 100,000.00 civil indemnity, PHP 100,000.00 moral damages, PHP 100,000.00 exemplary damages and PHP 50,000.00 temperate damages, all earning 6% interest per annum from finality of the decision until fully paid. The award of actual damages was DELETED. Criminal Case No. 6621 was DISMISSED as to Rudy Peralta y Mabbonag because of his death.

bar_questions.q: Nestor was charged with frustrated murder for treacherously stabbing Oscar. Two weeks later, before Nestor's arraignment, Oscar died of his wounds. The prosecutor filed an Amended Information charging Nestor with murder, with the same allegations plus the fact of Oscar's death. The court never issued an order admitting the Amended Information. Nestor was arraigned and pleaded not guilty "to the crime charged." After the prosecution rested, Nestor argued that without an order admitting the Amended Information, the only charge pending against him is frustrated murder, so he cannot be convicted of murder. Is Nestor correct?

alac.answer: No. The Amended Information for murder superseded the original Information when it was filed. No order admitting it was necessary.
alac.legal_basis: Under Rule 110, Section 14 of the Rules of Court, a complaint or information may be amended, in form or in substance, without leave of court at any time before the accused enters his plea. The exception is an amendment that downgrades the offense or excludes an accused. Because an amendment before plea is a matter of right, the amended information ipso facto supersedes the original, without a motion to admit or an order admitting it; a later order of admission is a superfluity. (People v. Peralta, G.R. No. 257105, August 27, 2025)
alac.application: The Amended Information was filed before Nestor pleaded. It neither downgraded the offense nor dropped any accused; it changed frustrated murder to murder because of Oscar's death. It therefore needed no leave and no order of admission, and it superseded the original Information as soon as it was filed. Nestor was arraigned after the amendment, so the charge he answered was murder.
alac.conclusion: Nestor may be convicted of murder; the absence of an order admitting the Amended Information does not matter.

bar_questions.q: Paolo was charged with frustrated murder for shooting Quintin with treachery. Paolo was arraigned and pleaded not guilty. During trial, Quintin died of the gunshot wound. Over Paolo's objection, the court gave the prosecution leave to amend the Information to murder, alleging the same facts plus Quintin's death. Paolo argues that (a) the amendment is substantial and can no longer be made after his plea, and (b) in any event, he must be arraigned anew on the murder charge. Rule on both contentions.

alac.answer: (a) The amendment is valid. It is only a formal amendment, which may be made after plea with leave of court. (b) Paolo need not be arraigned anew.
alac.legal_basis: Under Rule 110, Section 14, after the plea and during trial, a formal amendment may be made only with leave of court and when it can be done without prejudice to the rights of the accused. Amending frustrated murder to murder because the victim later died is merely formal. Frustrated murder is a stage of murder and is necessarily included in it, the death bears only on the penalty, and every defense under the original information remains available (Teehankee, Jr. v. Madayag, reiterated in People v. Peralta, G.R. No. 257105, August 27, 2025). Unlike a substantial amendment, a formal amendment does not require a second arraignment, because the purpose of arraignment was already served at the first one (People v. Peralta).
alac.application: (a) The Amended Information charges the same offense at a later stage of execution. The prosecution's theory, a shooting with intent to kill and treachery, is unchanged, and any defense Paolo had against frustrated murder applies equally to murder. The amendment is formal, and since the court gave leave and Paolo suffers no prejudice, it is allowed even during trial; his objection does not bar it. (b) Paolo was informed of the nature and cause of the accusation at his first arraignment. The amendment charges no new offense and cannot surprise him, so re-arraignment is unnecessary. A new preliminary investigation is likewise not required for a formal amendment.
alac.conclusion: The amendment to murder is valid, and Paolo may be tried and convicted of murder without a new arraignment.

bar_questions.q: The RTC convicted Rico of murder and ordered him to pay the victim's heirs civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages. The CA affirmed. While Rico's appeal to the Supreme Court was pending, he died in prison. The victim's heirs asked the Supreme Court to affirm the judgment at least as to the damages, so they could collect from Rico's estate. (a) What is the effect of Rico's death on his criminal liability and on his civil liability arising from the crime? (b) Do the heirs have any remaining recourse?

alac.answer: (a) Rico's criminal liability and his civil liability ex delicto are both totally extinguished, and the case must be dismissed as to him. (b) The heirs may pursue only civil liability based on sources of obligation other than the crime, if any exist.
alac.legal_basis: Under Article 89(1) of the Revised Penal Code, the death of the convict totally extinguishes criminal liability as to personal penalties, and as to pecuniary penalties when death occurs before final judgment. Death before final judgment also extinguishes civil liability ex delicto, but claims for civil liability based on other sources of obligation remain unaffected (People v. Bayotas). This was applied in People v. Peralta (G.R. No. 257105, August 27, 2025), where the case was dismissed as to an accused-appellant who died while his appeal was pending.
alac.application: Rico died while his appeal was pending, before any final judgment. His criminal liability and the civil liability arising solely from the murder are extinguished. The Court must therefore dismiss the case as to him rather than affirm the award of damages. If the heirs have a claim against Rico based on another source of obligation, such as law, contract, quasi-contract or quasi-delict, that claim survives his death and may still be pursued against his estate.
alac.conclusion: Rico's death pending appeal extinguishes his criminal liability and his civil liability ex delicto, leaving the heirs only claims based on other sources of obligation.

notes: The short title follows the first-named accused-appellant. Peralta died pending appeal, so the conviction stands only against Liban. Philip Soriano did not appeal to the Supreme Court, and a partial entry of judgment was issued as to him. The body quotes the older text of Rule 110, Section 14; footnote 38 quotes the current text, including the paragraph on amendments before plea that downgrade the offense or exclude an accused. Footnote 24 notes two versions of the RTC Judgment, one quoting the frustrated-murder Information and one quoting the Amended Information; both convict for murder. The E-Library text cites the parole guidelines as "A.M. No. 15-08-0-SC" (apparently truncated), so the digest refers to them by title. The victim AAA is anonymized in the decision.
